newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Belgrade tensions mount ahead of demonstrations.
newsitem.headline: Belgrade tensions mount ahead of demonstrations.

text.p: Socialist supporters shouted insults outside the offices of the Zajedno opposition coalition on Tuesday as tensions flared in Belgrade ahead of a socialist rally in support of Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic.

The authorities, who ferried demonstraters by bus from across the country, planned to hold their show of strength in the place where Zajedno (Together) has held 35 days of protests against alleged socialist election fraud.

Faced with the explosive prospect of rival demonstrations mingling in the street under the eyes of riot police, opposition spokesman Slobodan Vuksanovic said Zajedno might be forced to call off its demonstration.
"I don't know if there will be a march today or if there will be any (opposition) rallies for that matter. There seems to be chaos on the streets already.

Some 40,000 students, who have been holding parallel demonstrations against Milosevic, gathered about 1,000 metres (yards) from the Zajedno offices and said they would avoid all contact with the socialist rally.
The independent Beta news agency quoted a Socialist Party (SPS) source as saying Milosevic might speak at his supporters' demonstration "if enough people gather."

Zajedno, backed by the U.S. and other Western countries, is trying to force Milosevic to admit its victories in Belgrade and 14 other towns at local elections on November 17, breaking half a century of socialist rule.
Its peaceful daily demonstrations, which reached a peak of 250,000 people, have grown into the worst crisis the authoritarian Milosevic has faced in nine years of power.

Tuesday threatened to be a crunch day for both sides with Zajendo fearing SPS demonstrators would foment violence to give Milosevic an excuse to unleash his riot police or even call a state of emergency.
Vuksanovic told Reuters: "(Milosevic) is out of his mind. He has brought thousands of people to Belgrade, people who are not informed about this situation.
"In some part of Belgrade, they have already started fights. I am afraid it could be the beginning of civil war in Serbia and all responsibility is on Milosevic's side."

Vuksanovic said the SPS crowd shouting outside Zajedno's headquarters three hours before the demonstration was due to begin, were from the Pec, a hardline nationalist redoubt in the southern republic of Kosovo.
Kosovo Serbs were the shock troops who brought Milosevic to power on a tide of nationalism that set off the disintegration of former Yugoslavia in 1991-92.
Up to 10,000 other pro-Milosevic demonstrators were milling in the nearby Republic Square in case Zajedno switched its protest there.
As the atmosphere of intimdation grew, a party in the Zajedno coalition said its Belgrade bookshop was attacked by a group of unidentified men, at least three of them armed.
Zajedno earlier rejected an appeal by Serbian Orthodox Patriarch Pavle to suspend its demonstration after he warned that the conflict risked turning into an armed confrontation.
In a swipe at Milosevic, he coupled his plea with praise for the opposition's restraint during the campaign of protests.

Zajedno was told that the SPS had mobilised 10,000 buses to bring demonstrators, including factory workers, for "a spontaneous assembly of supporters of the peaceful and consistent policy of President Milosevic". The buses travelled under police escort.
Opposition sources said factory hands were threatened with reprisals, including the withdrawal of lay-off pay, if they refused to attend the socialist rally.

Although the opposition rallies in Belgrade and other towns have been peaceful, BETA reported scuffles on Monday in Valjevo, near Belgrade, when 20,000 Zajedno activists took to the streets in response to a socialist rally.
The last political street violence seen in Serbia was in 1991 when Milosevic used tanks to drive protesters off the streets and two lives were lost.
